content.title: About
content.content: Butter replacement, liquid is a plant‑based liquid butter substitute designed for culinary and bakery applications. The product is formulated from a blend of vegetable oils, emulsifiers and flavorings to mimic the taste and texture of traditional butter while containing less saturated fat and no dairy ingredients.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The product is suitable for vegans and people with lactose intolerance.
Its liquid form makes dosing and even distribution in doughs and sauces easy.
Trans‑fat content is minimized through modern oil processing techniques.
Butter replacement, liquid is often used in restaurants and food manufacturing to lower the calorie content of dishes.
Packaging is made from recyclable plastic to reduce environmental impact.

items.title: Low in saturated fat
items.content: Unlike traditional butter, the product contains mainly monounsaturated and polyunsaturated fatty acids, which support cardiovascular health.

items.title: Cholesterol‑free
items.content: Being plant‑based, it contains zero cholesterol, beneficial for individuals with elevated lipid levels.

items.title: Vitamin E content
items.content: Added tocopherols act as antioxidants, protecting cells from oxidative stress.

items.title: Allergy‑friendly
items.content: The absence of dairy proteins makes it safe for people with milk allergies.

items.title: Convenient to use
items.content: The liquid consistency simplifies incorporation into batters and sauces, yielding smooth, lump‑free results.

items.title: Allergy to vegetable oils
items.content: Some individuals may react to soy or sunflower oil, common ingredients in the formula.

items.title: Caloric density
items.content: Despite a healthier fat profile, the product is still calorie‑dense and should be used in moderation.

items.title: Not ideal for strict keto diets
items.content: Carbohydrate content can be higher than pure butter, limiting its use in very low‑carb regimens.

items.title: Heat stability
items.content: Prolonged heating above 180 °C may degrade emulsifiers, altering flavor and texture.

content.title: How to Use
content.content: Butter replacement, liquid can be used in baking, sauces, dressings, marinades and for sautéing. Replace butter 1:1 by volume in most recipes. When cooking at high heat, add the product toward the end of cooking to prevent separation.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store in a cool, dry place away from direct sunlight. After opening, keep refrigerated and use within 3 months. Discard if you notice off‑odors or color changes.

content.title: About
content.content: Cereal is a sweetened oat cereal coated with a sugary glaze and dotted with soft marshmallows. The oats are whole‑grain, toasted to a crisp texture, then glazed and topped with marshmallow pieces. It is marketed as a quick breakfast or snack.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The first commercial sweetened cereals appeared in the United States in the 1950s.
Marshmallows are added for a contrasting chewy texture and extra sweetness.
The glaze typically contains sugar, corn syrup, and flavorings such as vanilla.
Oat flakes provide complex carbohydrates that give lasting satiety.
The product is often advertised as a "fun breakfast" for kids but is enjoyed by adults as well.

items.title: Energy source
items.content: Oat flakes supply quick‑release carbohydrates for immediate energy, while the glaze adds fast‑acting calories.

items.title: Source of fiber
items.content: Oats contain soluble and insoluble fiber that supports healthy digestion.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: The cereal provides thiamine, riboflavin, and niacin, which are important for metabolism.

items.title: Minerals
items.content: Oats contribute iron, magnesium, and phosphorus, essential for bone health and blood formation.

items.title: Mood boost
items.content: The sweet taste and soft marshmallow texture can improve mood and increase satisfaction with the meal.

items.title: High sugar content
items.content: The glaze and marshmallows make the product very sweet, which can contribute to weight gain and increase the risk of tooth decay.

items.title: Gluten allergy
items.content: Oat cereals are often processed on equipment that handles wheat, making them unsuitable for people with celiac disease.

items.title: Additive content
items.content: Artificial flavors and preservatives may be present, which some consumers prefer to avoid.

items.title: Choking hazard for young children
items.content: Soft, sticky marshmallows can pose a choking risk for small children.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Typically eaten dry with milk or yogurt. It can also be microwaved briefly so the glaze softens and the marshmallows become more pliable. Pairing with berries or nuts can reduce overall sweetness.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store the package in a cool, dry place and reseal tightly after opening. For longer storage, transfer to an airtight container to prevent moisture absorption and loss of crunch.

content.title: About
content.content: Dry cottage cheese (dry curd) is a dehydrated cheese made from skimmed milk. It has a fine crumbly texture, low moisture, and a pronounced milky flavor. It is used in cooking for fillings, baked goods, desserts, and as a high‑protein ingredient.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Dry curd is a staple in many Eastern European dishes such as pierogi and syrniki.
Because the water is removed, it contains almost twice the protein of regular cottage cheese.
When sealed, it can be stored at room temperature for up to 12 months.
Unlike processed cheese spreads, dry curd contains no additives, flavorings or preservatives.

items.title: Rich in protein
items.content: Dry curd provides high‑quality protein essential for muscle growth and repair.

items.title: Low in fat
items.content: Being made from skimmed milk, it has minimal fat, making it suitable for low‑calorie diets.

items.title: Source of calcium
items.content: Calcium supports bone and teeth health and plays a role in nerve function.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: It contains vitamin B12 and riboflavin, important for energy metabolism.

items.title: Digestive tolerance
items.content: Lactose levels are low, which can be easier to digest for people with mild lactose intolerance.

items.title: Milk protein allergy
items.content: Individuals allergic to casein or whey may react to dry curd.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: Some varieties are salted; people monitoring sodium intake should check the label.

items.title: Possible contamination
items.content: Improper storage can lead to mold growth; keep the package sealed.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Dry curd can be mixed into dough for breads and pastries, used as a filling for pies, dumplings, pancakes, or blended into protein smoothies. It also works well sprinkled over yogurt or combined with fruit and nuts.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store dry curd in a tightly sealed package in a cool, dry place. Once opened, keep it in the refrigerator and consume within 2–3 weeks.

content.title: About
content.content: Dried cherries are the dehydrated fruit of the sweet cherry tree (Prunus cerasus). They retain a characteristic sweet‑tart flavor, bright red color, and a chewy texture, while offering a longer shelf life compared to fresh cherries.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Cherries belong to the Rosaceae family and are closely related to plums, apricots, and almonds.
Dried cherries are often used as a convenient substitute for fresh fruit in baking and desserts.
The drying process concentrates anthocyanins, giving the berries their vivid color.
Historically, dried cherries have been used in folk medicine to aid digestion.
They are easier to transport and store than fresh cherries.

items.title: Rich in antioxidants
items.content: Dried cherries contain anthocyanins and vitamin C, which help protect cells from oxidative stress.

items.title: Supports digestion
items.content: Dietary fiber in cherries promotes regular bowel movements and can help relieve constipation.

items.title: Source of potassium
items.content: Potassium assists in fluid balance and supports heart function.

items.title: Low in fat
items.content: Unlike many nuts, dried cherries contain virtually no fat, making them suitable for low‑fat diets.

items.title: Immune system support
items.content: Vitamin C and other phytochemicals contribute to a stronger immune response.

items.title: High natural sugar
items.content: Drying concentrates the fruit's natural sugars, so dried cherries can be calorie‑dense and may affect blood sugar levels.

items.title: Cherry allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to cherries, ranging from skin rashes to swelling.

items.title: Sulfite content
items.content: Sulfites are sometimes added to preserve color and freshness, which can cause reactions in sulfite‑sensitive people.

items.title: Dental concerns
items.content: The sticky texture can adhere to teeth and increase the risk of cavities if consumed frequently.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Dried cherries can be enjoyed as a snack, added to oatmeal, yogurt, baked goods, salads, or used in sauces and marmalades. Soaking them in water or juice softens the texture if desired.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store dried cherries in an airtight container in a cool, dry, dark place. For extended storage, keep them in the refrigerator. Discard any that develop off‑odors, discoloration, or mold.

content.title: About
content.content: Chocolate candy is a small sweet made from chocolate, sugar, dairy ingredients and sometimes add‑ins such as nuts, dried fruit or caramel. It can be coated, filled or have a center, and is often enjoyed as a dessert or treat.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The first chocolate bar was created in 1847 in England.
Chocolate candies are popular gifts for holidays, especially Valentine’s Day and Christmas.
Dark chocolate contains more cocoa and less sugar than milk chocolate, giving it a more bitter taste but potentially more health benefits.
In some cultures “chocolate coins” are given as symbols of wealth during celebrations.
Vegan chocolate candies exist, using plant‑based milks and fats instead of dairy.

items.title: Rich in antioxidants
items.content: Dark chocolate is high in flavonoids, which help combat free radicals.

items.title: Supports cardiovascular health
items.content: Moderate consumption of dark chocolate may improve vessel elasticity and lower blood pressure.

items.title: Source of magnesium
items.content: Magnesium in chocolate supports muscle and nerve function.

items.title: Mood enhancement
items.content: Chocolate stimulates serotonin and endorphin production, improving mood.

items.title: Quick energy boost
items.content: Sugar and fat in candy provide rapid energy.

items.title: High sugar content
items.content: Excessive intake can contribute to weight gain and increase the risk of cavities.

items.title: Milk protein allergy
items.content: Milk chocolate may trigger allergic reactions in people with lactose intolerance or milk protein allergy.

items.title: Caffeine and theobromine
items.content: Chocolate contains stimulants that can cause insomnia or rapid heartbeat when consumed in large amounts.

items.title: Trans‑fat presence
items.content: Some commercial candies may contain partially hydrogenated oils, which are harmful to heart health.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Chocolate candy can be enjoyed on its own, added to baked goods, desserts, or used as a garnish for cakes. It is often served at room temperature so the chocolate stays soft and aromatic.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store candies in a dry, cool place in an airtight container, away from direct sunlight. Above 20 °C the chocolate may melt, while low temperatures can cause condensation that changes texture.

cookie-vanilla-with-caramel-coconut-and-.title: Cookie, vanilla with caramel, coconut, and chocolate coating

content.title: About
content.content: A soft cookie flavored with aromatic vanilla, drizzled with caramel sauce, sprinkled with coconut flakes, and coated in a crisp chocolate glaze. The perfect blend of sweetness and texture for dessert lovers.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Vanilla‑caramel pairing is a classic in confectionery for creating depth of flavor.
Coconut flakes add a light tropical note and a crunchy texture.
Chocolate coating gives the cookie a glossy finish and enhances the vanilla aroma.
Often served with tea or coffee as a sweet snack.
The recipe was created in the early 2020s as part of a premium dessert line.

items.title: Energy source
items.content: Sugars from caramel and chocolate quickly replenish glucose stores, providing a rapid energy boost.

items.title: Antioxidants
items.content: Chocolate contains flavonoids that help combat free radicals.

items.title: Small amount of protein
items.content: Vanilla extract and coconut flakes provide modest protein useful for tissue repair.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: The product includes trace amounts of B1 and B2 vitamins, supporting metabolism.

items.title: Minerals
items.content: Coconut flakes supply magnesium and iron, important for nervous and blood health.

items.title: High sugar content
items.content: Large amounts of sugar can contribute to weight gain and increase the risk of cavities.

items.title: Coconut allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to coconut flakes.

items.title: Caffeine in chocolate
items.content: Dark chocolate contains small amounts of caffeine, which may affect sensitive individuals.

items.title: Caloric density
items.content: The cookie is fairly calorie‑dense, so moderate consumption is recommended.

items.title: Gluten content
items.content: Traditional dough contains wheat, making it unsuitable for people with celiac disease.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Enjoy the cookie as a standalone treat, crumble it into ice cream, use it in layered cakes, or pair it with a hot beverage.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store in an airtight container in a cool, dry place. For longer shelf life, keep refrigerated to prevent the chocolate coating from melting.

manicotti-cheese-filled-with-tomato-sauc.title: Manicotti, cheese‑filled with tomato sauce, meatless

content.title: About
content.content: Manicotti are large tube‑shaped pasta shells stuffed with creamy cheese and baked in a flavorful tomato sauce. This vegetarian dish contains no meat but delivers a rich taste thanks to the combination of cheese, tomatoes, basil and spices.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The name “manicotti” comes from the Italian word “manicotto,” meaning “sleeve” or “hand‑tube.”
Traditional fillings include ricotta, mozzarella and parmesan, though other cheeses can be used.
The tomato sauce is often cooked with olive oil, garlic and oregano, giving the dish a Mediterranean aroma.
Manicotti is popular in the US and Canada as a convenient quick‑dinner option that reheats easily in the oven.
It is frequently garnished with fresh basil or parsley for a bright color contrast.

items.title: Rich in calcium
items.content: The cheese filling provides a high level of calcium, essential for bone and tooth health.

items.title: Good source of protein
items.content: Cheese and dairy deliver complete protein that supports tissue repair and maintenance.

items.title: Lycopene in tomato sauce
items.content: Tomatoes contain lycopene, a powerful antioxidant that supports cardiovascular health.

items.title: Moderate saturated fat
items.content: Using low‑fat cheese varieties can keep the dish relatively low in saturated fat and calories.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Cheese and fortified pasta supply B1, B2 and B12 vitamins, important for energy metabolism.

items.title: Lactose intolerance
items.content: Dairy ingredients may cause discomfort for people who are lactose intolerant.

items.title: Milk‑protein allergy
items.content: Cheese can be an allergen for individuals allergic to casein.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: Tomato sauce and cheese often contain added salt; those monitoring sodium intake should watch portion size.

items.title: Gluten
items.content: Traditional wheat pasta contains gluten; a gluten‑free version is needed for people with celiac disease.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve manicotti hot, straight from the oven. Garnish with fresh basil, grated parmesan or a pinch of red pepper flakes. The dish is eaten with a fork and knife and works well as individual portions in fast‑casual restaurants.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep cooked manicotti in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 3‑4 days. For longer storage, freeze in a freezer‑safe bag for up to 2 months. Reheat until the internal temperature reaches 75 °C.

content.title: About
content.content: Orange juice 100 % is a completely natural juice obtained from ripe oranges, frozen immediately after pressing and later reconstituted with water to its original volume. This processing preserves most of the vitamins and the fresh‑juice flavor.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Freezing right after pressing retains up to 90 % of vitamin C, which degrades quickly in liquid juice.
Reconstituted juice tastes like fresh‑pressed juice but can be stored frozen for up to 12 months.
Orange juice is widely used in sauces, marinades, and desserts.
Juice from the ‘Valencia’ orange variety is considered the sweetest and most aromatic.
In the United States, more than 30 % of all frozen fruit juices are orange juice.

items.title: Rich in vitamin C
items.content: Vitamin C supports the immune system, aids collagen synthesis, and acts as a powerful antioxidant.

items.title: Contains folate
items.content: Folate is essential for DNA synthesis and is especially important for pregnant women.

items.title: Source of potassium
items.content: Potassium helps regulate blood pressure and supports heart function.

items.title: Low in fat
items.content: The juice contains virtually no fat, making it suitable for low‑calorie diets.

items.title: Antioxidants
items.content: In addition to vitamin C, the juice provides flavonoids that protect cells from oxidative stress.

items.title: Citrus allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to oranges.

items.title: Acidity
items.content: High acidity can irritate the stomach lining in people with gastritis or ulcers.

items.title: Sugar content
items.content: Although no sugar is added, natural sugars can affect blood glucose levels.

items.title: Vitamin loss with improper storage
items.content: If the juice is thawed and kept at room temperature for more than 24 hours, a portion of the vitamins degrades.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: The juice can be enjoyed on its own, used in smoothies, cocktails, sauces, and marinades. When reconstituting, add clean water in a 1:1 volume ratio, mix thoroughly, and chill before serving.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store the frozen juice at –18 °C in an airtight package. After thawing, keep it in the refrigerator for no more than 2‑3 days and consume within 24 hours of opening.

rice-white-with-peas-and-carrots-no-adde.title: White Rice with Peas and Carrots, No Added Fat

content.title: About
content.content: This dish consists of boiled white rice, cooked green peas and carrots, prepared without any added fat. It is commonly served in child nutrition programs, diet menus, and institutional catering as a source of easily digestible carbohydrates, protein, and vitamins.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: White rice is a staple energy source in many countries.
Peas are rich in plant protein and fiber, while carrots provide provitamin A.
A fat‑free preparation fits low‑calorie dietary plans.
Rice with vegetables is traditionally cooked in Asian cuisines, valued for taste and nutrition.
When stored properly, the prepared dish stays fresh for up to 3 days in the refrigerator.

items.title: Source of complex carbs
items.content: White rice delivers a steady supply of glucose, helping maintain energy levels.

items.title: Rich in plant protein
items.content: Peas add about 5 g of protein per 100 g of the dish.

items.title: Vitamins and minerals
items.content: Carrots provide beta‑carotene, and peas supply iron and folate.

items.title: Low in fat
items.content: The absence of added fats makes the meal suitable for cardiovascular health.

items.title: Supports digestion
items.content: Fiber from peas and carrots promotes regular bowel function.

items.title: High glycemic index
items.content: White rice can raise blood sugar quickly, so people with diabetes should monitor portion sizes.

items.title: Pea allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to peas.

items.title: Lack of fats
items.content: Without fats, the absorption of fat‑soluble vitamins may be reduced; consider adding a small amount of healthy fat elsewhere in the diet.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve the dish as a standalone meal or as a side to meat, fish, or tofu. It reheats well in the microwave or on the stovetop with a splash of water to prevent drying out.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep the prepared product in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 3 days. For longer storage, freeze portions for up to 1 month, thawing them in the fridge before serving.

content.title: About
content.content: Fruit flavored water beverage is a non‑alcoholic drink made by adding natural or artificial flavorings to pure drinking water. The beverage contains no sugar, calories, or caffeine, yet delivers a bright fruit taste that makes it popular among both children and adults looking for a refreshing, light option.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Fruit flavored water is often used as an alternative to sweet carbonated sodas.
Flavorings can be derived from real fruit juice, but most commercial products use concentrated extracts.
Some brands fortify the drink with vitamin C (ascorbic acid) to enhance taste and extend shelf life.
The beverage is available in both sparkling and still versions.
In many markets it is sold in 0.5 L and 1.5 L bottles.

items.title: Hydration
items.content: Like plain water, the drink helps maintain the body’s fluid balance.

items.title: Low Calorie Content
items.content: The absence of sugar makes it suitable for calorie‑restricted diets.

items.title: Vitamin C (in some variants)
items.content: Added vitamin C supports the immune system and acts as an antioxidant.

items.title: Caffeine‑Free
items.content: Ideal for children and individuals avoiding stimulants.

items.title: Easy on the Stomach
items.content: Most variants have low acidity, which is gentle on the digestive tract.

items.title: Allergy to Flavorings
items.content: Some people may experience allergic reactions to artificial flavorings or added additives.

items.title: Acidity
items.content: Certain versions can be slightly acidic, potentially affecting tooth enamel with frequent consumption.

items.title: Preservatives
items.content: Preservatives used to extend shelf life may not be suitable for individuals with sensitivities.

content.title: How to Drink
content.content: Serve chilled, optionally with ice or a slice of fresh fruit to boost flavor. It works well as a standalone refresher or as a base for non‑alcoholic cocktails.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store in a cool, dry place away from direct sunlight. After opening, keep refrigerated and consume within 3–5 days.

content.title: About
content.content: Whiskey and cola is a popular mixed drink made from aged whiskey and carbonated cola. The beverage combines the woody, vanilla and caramel notes of whiskey with the sweet and slightly bitter flavor of cola, creating a refreshing and balanced taste.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The whiskey‑and‑cola cocktail originated in the United States in the early 1920s and quickly became a favorite among young adults.
Mixing whiskey with cola is believed to soften the harshness of the spirit, making it more approachable for a wider audience.
Different countries use different cola brands: in the US the classic Coca‑Cola is typical, while in Europe lighter variants such as Schweppes Cola are sometimes preferred.
It is customary to serve whiskey and cola over ice in tall glasses, often garnished with a lemon or lime wedge.
In the 1970s, whiskey brands ran advertising campaigns that highlighted the drink as part of a lively social scene, frequently featuring the mixed version with cola.

items.title: Contains antioxidants
items.content: Aged whiskey, especially when matured in oak barrels, contains polyphenols that may have antioxidant properties.

items.title: Moderate consumption may promote relaxation
items.content: Small amounts of alcohol can help reduce stress and improve mood.

items.title: Provides B‑vitamins
items.content: Whiskey contains thiamine, riboflavin and niacin, which are involved in energy metabolism.

items.title: Alcohol intoxication
items.content: Excessive consumption of whiskey leads to intoxication, increased risk of injury and long‑term health issues.

items.title: High sugar content in cola
items.content: Cola adds a significant amount of sugar, which can contribute to weight gain and elevated blood glucose levels.

items.title: Interaction with medications
items.content: Alcohol can amplify the effects of certain medicines, so it should be limited or avoided when taking medication.

content.title: How to Drink
content.content: Pour 40–50 ml of whiskey into a tall glass, add ice, and top up with cola. Optionally garnish with a lemon or lime wedge. Sip slowly and enjoy the aroma.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store the whiskey bottle in a cool, dark place with the cap tightly sealed. Keep opened cola refrigerated to maintain carbonation.
